1.text:
The flag of Tonga consists of a red field with a white canton in the upper left corner containing a centered red cross. Assigning value \(a\) to every red pixel and value \(b\) to every white pixel therefore produces a matrix \(M\) whose entries take only these two values.

Partition the rows of \(M\) according to the flag's geometry:
- Any row lying entirely outside the canton is uniformly red, hence consists of the constant vector whose every entry equals \(a\).
- Any row that intersects the canton but lies inside the horizontal bar of the cross is likewise uniformly red (the cross itself is red), again yielding the constant vector of all \(a\)'s.
- Any row that intersects the canton but lies outside the horizontal bar of the cross has white pixels precisely in the two segments of the canton that avoid the vertical bar of the cross; every other entry is red. Consequently every such row is identical to one fixed non-constant vector whose pattern is completely determined by the (fixed) column extents of the canton and the vertical bar.

Thus \(M\) contains at most two distinct row vectors. The row space is therefore at most two-dimensional, which implies
\[
\operatorname{rank}(M)\le 2.
\]
When \(a\neq b\) the two row vectors are linearly independent, so the bound is attained. Because the argument relies only on the rectangular geometry of the colored regions and not on any particular pixel resolution, the rank cannot exceed 2 for any discretization of the flag.

Hence the maximal possible rank is 2.
